name: Jade Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run Kestrel Farm with my dad, Hiro. It's 260 hectares, 900 ewes, wheat and oats, and we've got a farm shop and a small butchery on the main road into town. Dad does the sheep work with me, but the planning, the shop and the money side are mine now. I'm in the lambing shed or the fields by half six, then at the shop by eleven, then back out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's ours and that people drive out to buy our lamb because they know us. I use AI every day: for the accounts, the shop's social media, lambing records, even working out the butchery rota. We're trialling GPS collars on the ewes that let you move them with a virtual fence on your phone. What wears me out is the hours. The shop's open six days and sheep don't do weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use what works and ignore the rest. I'd probably post a video from the shop about how we use it for small jobs. People like seeing a real farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine with me. We're already using the useful bits. If everyone else doesn't bother, we keep our head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as we are, keep the collars if the trial works, and push on with the plan to open a second shop counter at the garden centre in town. That's about thirty thousand, half from my savings, half from the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, which is normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The GPS collars, do they stay in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they pay their way, yes. So far they've saved Dad about two hours a day walking the hill. He complained for a week and now he shows them off to the neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be working on next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second counter, and getting Dad to take a proper day off. He's 61 and he hasn't had a weekend since my mother's funeral.

S0.say: Use what works and ignore the rest. I'd post a video from the shop about how we use it for small jobs, because people like seeing a real farm.
S0.think: It's fine with me, because we're already using the useful bits. If everyone else doesn't bother, we keep our head start.
S0.do: Keeps the farm running as now and keeps the GPS collars if the trial pays. Opens a second shop counter at a garden centre for about thirty thousand, half from her savings and half from the business.
S0.quote: He complained for a week and now he shows them off to the neighbours.
S0.fieldNote: Jade already blends tradition and technology: a family farm and butchery run with daily AI tools. Her plans are about growing the business. A quiet sadness shows when she mentions her father not taking a weekend since her mother's death.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say family farms that move early will do well, and nobody should wait for a government scheme to save them. I'd show what we're doing on the shop's page. Lots of people would rather learn from another farmer than an advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for us. We own the land and the business, so if machines make the work cheaper, the gain is ours. I'd just need to keep the shop personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd make the collars permanent, get a robot for the oat field weeding if one exists for hilly ground, and put the shop's ordering online with AI handling the stock. About forty thousand in all. I'd use savings for most of it rather than borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring in first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The butchery stock system, because it's a mess. Then the sheep handling. I'd keep Kai, our butcher, front and centre. Customers come for him as much as the lamb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your customers are people with jobs too. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If people round here are changing jobs, they might spend less on good meat. But most still have work in this picture, so I'd keep prices fair and keep the shop friendly.

S1.say: Family farms that move early will do well, and nobody should wait for a government scheme to save them. I'd show on the shop's page what we're doing so other farmers can learn.
S1.think: It's good for us, because we own the land and the business, so if machines make the work cheaper the gain is ours. I'd just need to keep the shop personal.
S1.do: Makes the GPS collars permanent, looks for a weeding robot for hilly ground and moves the shop's ordering online with AI managing stock. Spends about forty thousand, mostly from savings rather than borrowing.
S1.quote: I'd keep Kai, our butcher, front and centre. Customers come for him as much as the lamb.
S1.fieldNote: Ownership shapes her view: cheaper work means gains for her family. She's careful to keep the human face of the shop, naming the butcher as part of what customers buy. She prefers paying from savings over debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's every family for itself for a while, so look after your own and your neighbours. I'd also say don't let the government take over everything in a panic. People will need to stand on their own feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be all right as owners, better than most. But two years is fast, and our shop lives on local people having money. If half the town loses its work at once, who buys a leg of lamb?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate everything on the farm I could in the first year, so our costs drop before prices fall. I'd keep the shop but change it, cheaper cuts, bigger family packs. I'd pay off the small loan on the butchery so we owe nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for the farm, more for the shop and the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You own the farm. So what's the worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The customers. A farm without a shop just sells to a big buyer at whatever price they set. The shop is what makes us more than a supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the hill is ours and nobody can take it. That he'd finally get his weekends, because a robot would do the feed round. He'd say, I don't want weekends, I want sheep. And he'd still be out there.

S2.say: It's every family for itself for a while, so look after your own and your neighbours. Don't let the government take over everything in a panic, because people will need to stand on their own feet.
S2.think: We'd be all right as owners, better than most. But our shop lives on local people having money, and if half the town loses its work at once, who buys a leg of lamb?
S2.do: Automates as much of the farm as she can in the first year to cut costs before prices fall. Pays off the small butchery loan and changes the shop to cheaper cuts and family packs.
S2.feel: Uneasy, mainly for the shop and the town rather than the farm.
S2.quote: If half the town loses its work at once, who buys a leg of lamb?
S2.fieldNote: She doesn't fear the robots; she fears her customers losing their income. Her money moves are about owing nothing and cutting costs fast. The exchange with her father is affectionate and shows who he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so families and small businesses should start now. Learn the tools, cut debt, own what you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is good for us. Long enough to build up the shop and online sales, short enough that we'd be ahead of most farms around us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the sheep work over the first two years and use the time saved to grow the shop and start a delivery round to the towns nearby. I'd buy the 30 hectares next door if it came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of pressure, the good kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build instead of brace. In the fast one I'd be cutting and protecting. With five years I could grow first, then tighten up just before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I've got a habit of thinking every change is a chance. Dad says I'd see a flood and start selling boats. But we have the land and the savings, so being a bit wrong wouldn't sink us.

S3.say: Five years is time to get ready, so families and small businesses should start now: learn the tools, cut debt and own what you can.
S3.think: Five years is good for us, long enough to build up the shop and online sales and short enough that we'd be ahead of most farms around us.
S3.do: Automates the sheep work over two years and uses the saved time to grow the shop and start a delivery round to nearby towns. Buys 30 neighbouring hectares if they come up for sale.
S3.feel: Calm, with a healthy kind of pressure.
S3.quote: Dad says I'd see a flood and start selling boats.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years let her grow first and protect later. She knows her own optimism can be a weakness and laughs at it through her father's line. Land and savings make her comfortable taking that risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to prepare. Teach your kids a trade, keep your family close, own something. That's what I'd tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the easiest of the lot for us. We'd adopt at a sensible pace and grow the shop. By the time it lands, we'd already be running with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now with a longer plan. Collars, then a weeding robot, then more robots as they get cheaper. Second shop counter, delivery round. Keep saving a good share of the profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 37. Where would you want to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running Kestrel with robots doing the heavy work and people doing the shop, the butchery and the deciding. Maybe married with kids, if I ever find the time to meet anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long version change how you think about family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want my own kids to grow up knowing how to handle a ewe, even if they never need to. And I'd want them to understand that the land is what lasts, not the machines.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for anyone to prepare. Teach your kids a trade, keep your family close and own something.
S4.think: It's the easiest of the lot for us, because we'd adopt at a sensible pace and grow the shop. By the time it lands we'd already be running with robots.
S4.do: Follows a longer version of her current plan: collars, then a weeding robot, then more robots as prices fall, plus the second shop counter and a delivery round. Keeps saving a good share of profits.
S4.quote: Maybe married with kids, if I ever find the time to meet anyone.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years barely changes her plan; it only slows it. Her picture of the future keeps people in the shop and the decisions while robots do the heavy work. Family and passing on skills come up naturally at the end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because of the town, not the farm. If our customers lose their work all at once, a farm shop is the first thing they cut. What would help is keeping people in work locally, through apprenticeships and small businesses, not just cheques from the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who we sell to. People think farming is about the farmer. It's about the people who buy from you. A robot can grow lamb, but someone still has to want to buy it from us.

headlineQuote: A robot can grow lamb, but someone still has to want to buy it from us.
portrait: Jade Tanaka is a 27-year-old who runs her family's sheep and cereal farm with her father, plus a farm shop and butchery on the road into town. She uses AI every day for accounts, marketing and lambing records and is trialling GPS collars on the ewes. Her views are traditional and pro-market: own what you can, look after family, don't wait for government. She stays calm in most pictures because her family owns the land and business, and only the fast AGI picture makes her uneasy, because the shop depends on local people having money to spend.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because if customers lost their work all at once the farm shop would be the first thing they cut.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping people in work locally through apprenticeships and small businesses, rather than relying on government cheques.
